\title{The pathwidth complex}
\author{Alexandre Linhares\\{\small Getulio Vargas Foundation (on leave) and Argo Laboratory}\\{\small \href{mailto:alex@argolab.org}{alex@argolab.org} \quad ORCID \href{https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4227-6879}{0000-0002-4227-6879}} \and
Horacio Hideki Yanasse\\{\small Institute of Science and Technology, Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP), São José dos Campos, SP, Brazil}\\{\small \href{mailto:horacio.yanasse@unifesp.br}{horacio.yanasse@unifesp.br} \quad ORCID \href{https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6946-9670}{0000-0002-6946-9670}}}
\date{19 October 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
In 2001 we listed twelve problems from operations research, VLSI
design and graph theory, the minimization of open stacks problem (MOSP) among
them, as equal ``plus or minus one'', and gave no proofs
\citep{Linhares2001,LY2002}. We now correct and extend the table, proving formally in Lean that most of
them are, mathematically, one quantity, \emph{graph pathwidth}, studied
independently by communities that rarely cite one another. Eight rows are exact,
counting pathwidth itself: each equals pathwidth or pathwidth plus one. Two lie
in \emph{bands}: they stay within one or two of pathwidth, but not at a fixed
offset. Two are false as originally stated. We add three members the table missed:
(i) the maximum wavefront of sparse matrix elimination, which brings a fourth
discipline, numerical linear algebra, into the family; (ii) progressive
pebbling; and (iii) the vertex search of Bienstock, Robertson, Seymour and
Thomas. We call this cluster the
\emph{pathwidth complex}, as the literature uses the name \emph{pathwidth} more
than three times as often as the other eleven names combined. Since 2005, the
next most active name is MOSP, and the open-stacks community produced, by way
of that year's Constraint Modelling Challenge, the best exact algorithm for
MOSP: the \emph{customer search} of \citet{ChuStuckey2009}, which branches on the order in which customers' stacks close (also a
pathwidth algorithm). We prove in Lean that two of its published dominance theorems,
rules that discard a branch as no better than another, are \emph{not true},
and that on a 34-customer counter-example instance their algorithm, with its better move off, reports an
optimum of 7 where the optimum is 6. Our corrected search (and a SAT solver with a checked DRAT proof) confirms the 6. Our corrected definite move,
the first of the two, was also found by Tamaki as a lemma
\citep[Lemma~1]{Kitsunai2016} in the pathwidth literature; we prove our
corrected search sound, formally, in Lean. We re-prove all 115 benchmark
optima that rested on Chu and Stuckey's algorithm, changing none. Ported to graphs, our corrected search proves the pathwidth of all 11,534
Rome graphs, a standard graph-drawing benchmark of 10 to 110 vertices (97.1\% of them within 10 minutes each), and, on every benchmark set with published
exact counts, as many graphs or more than the published branch and bound of
Coudert, Mazauric and Nisse (2016). In the other direction, \emph{from pathwidth to MOSP}, a lower bound from graph
minors, proved in Lean, settles in seconds instances whose refutation took
core-days, and closes the Mycielski graph $M_7$. All of our proofs and solvers are open source.
We also release a dataset of 17,714 graphs, distinct up to isomorphism, from
twenty benchmark collections for pathwidth and the problems equal to it, the
MOSP instances and the Rome graphs among them, 16,634 of them with a certified
pathwidth, with independent checkers. We believe ours is currently the
strongest exact pathwidth solver openly available.
\end{abstract}
